mcqs.question: Why can MapReduce automatically parallelize and retry work across a cluster without the programmer writing distributed-systems code?
options: Because Hadoop clusters use specialized hardware that handles parallelism transparently
Because map and reduce are the only two operations allowed, so the framework fully controls scheduling, retries, and data movement around them
Because MapReduce jobs are limited to a single machine and don't actually need coordination
Because the programmer must manually specify which machine runs each task
mcqs.explanation: The restriction to exactly two operations is what lets the framework own everything around them — splitting input, scheduling tasks, retrying failures, and shuffling data — without the programmer's code needing to know about any of it. MapReduce runs across ordinary commodity clusters, not specialized hardware, and coordination is the framework's job, not something left to manual placement.

mcqs.question: What roles do the NameNode and DataNodes play in HDFS?
options: The NameNode stores all file data directly, and DataNodes only cache it temporarily
DataNodes hold the in-memory metadata for all files, and the NameNode stores the actual block data
The NameNode runs all MapReduce reduce tasks, and DataNodes only run map tasks
The NameNode holds file-to-block metadata in memory, while DataNodes store and serve the actual replicated blocks
mcqs.explanation: The split is metadata (NameNode, kept in memory for fast lookups) versus actual block storage and serving (DataNodes, where the real data and its replicas live). The other options invert or fabricate these responsibilities — the NameNode doesn't store file data itself, and node roles in HDFS aren't tied to which MapReduce task type runs where.

mcqs.question: Why does an iterative machine learning algorithm running 20 passes over the same dataset suffer disproportionately under MapReduce's execution model?
options: Because MapReduce cannot run the same algorithm more than once
Because each iteration is a separate MapReduce job, so the disk write/read round-trip on every stage is paid again on every single pass over the same data
Because HDFS deletes data after each MapReduce job completes
Because iterative algorithms require more replicas than HDFS allows
mcqs.explanation: Each pass is its own full job with its own disk round-trips at every map, shuffle, and reduce boundary, so a cost that's tolerable once gets paid again and again across iterations — that repetition is exactly what an in-memory engine eliminates. HDFS doesn't delete data between jobs, running the same job repeatedly is completely normal, and replication count is unrelated to how many iterations a job runs.

mcqs.question: What specifically enabled Spark's roughly 10-100x speedup over MapReduce on iterative machine learning workloads?
options: Spark keeping intermediate data in memory across stages and iterations, eliminating the repeated disk round-trips MapReduce pays on every pass
Spark running on faster physical hardware than Hadoop clusters typically used
Spark compressing data more aggressively than MapReduce did
Spark reducing the number of machines needed in the cluster
mcqs.explanation: The speedup is architectural, not about faster hardware or compression — it comes directly from removing the disk write/read cycle that MapReduce repeats on every iteration, which compounds heavily over many passes. Spark and Hadoop can and did run on comparable commodity clusters; the difference is what happens to intermediate data between stages, and cluster size isn't the driver of this speedup either.

mcqs.question: For what kind of workload does MapReduce's disk-bound execution model remain a reasonable fit even today?
options: Real-time streaming dashboards requiring sub-second latency
Iterative machine learning training over a dataset that fits in cluster memory
Interactive ad-hoc SQL exploration by an analyst
A genuinely single-pass batch job over data far larger than available cluster memory, with no repeated iteration to speed up by caching
mcqs.explanation: MapReduce's cost model only becomes a disadvantage when the same data is revisited repeatedly — for a true single-pass job over data too large to fit in memory anyway, there's no repeated-access cost an in-memory engine would actually save. Streaming, interactive SQL, and iterative ML are exactly the cases where in-memory engines' repeated-access advantage matters most, making them poor fits for MapReduce's model.
